quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Clayton Truan Brown was born in Red Deer on Jan.13th 1920.The second son of Lyle Edward and Josephine Brown. In between Tom and Ralph. They lived in Valley Centre where his father farmed the homestead settled in 1898 by his father Tom from Grundy Center Iowa. Three boys and hired men was a lively household with few conveniences.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text:
In 1928 they moved to Mitchener Hill, on the N.E. corner of 43rd, Ave. Red Deer so the boys could get a better education. The population was 2,800. Many happy memories of these days, including tobogganing down the hill and being brought up by a passing team and sleigh. Swimming in the creek below in the nude, and a paper route that took him from the then C.P.R. station to the Training School {now known as Mitchener Centre} setting snares along the way. He got 1 ½ cents a paper per week for 15 customers, but it cost 10 cents at the matinee and 5 cents for ½ lb of candy. He also remembers letting the saddle horse go and it finding its way home to the farm.

Clayton joined the cadets when he was 12. Trained by Joseph Welsh after school. He won a badge for top marks in the province for 22 shot and was 3rd, in the dominion. He joined the reserve in 1937, and in 1939 they won the Cunningham cup for the best all around battery on the firing range.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text:
Clayton joined the army on Sept 13th. 1939 in Calgary after having been rejected earlier for service on the west coast. The army paid him $1.25. He was working at North West Motors for $1 a day and sometimes had to wait for the money till a farmer paid his bill. He trained in Calgary for 4 months. where they became the 23rd, Battery 2nd, Anti-Tank Regiment.

His father Lyle was born in Grundy Center on Sept. 18th,1887 and died at 53 on Nov.28th 1939. His brothers both joined the Airforce. Tom was killed in June 1952 and Ralph died in May 1987.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text: As he was underweight, the army had a little trouble finding a place for him.

quotes.source: From the Red Deer Advocate, Nov. 29, 1939, “Death of L. E. Brown”
quotes.text:
Old friends will regret to hear of the death at Red Deer on Tuesday of L. E. Brown, in his 53rd year.

Lyle Edward Brown was born in Grundy Centre, Iowa, on September 13, 1887. He came here with his family in 1899 and they homesteaded on the present farm in Valley Centre.

On January 22, 1916, he was married to Miss Josephine Truan, who had been teaching at Balmoral, and there are three sons: Thomas, who operates the farm; Gnr. Creighton Brown, of the 23rd Battery, Calgary, and Ralph at home.

"Creighton" is the paper's mistake for Clayton. His father died eleven weeks after he enlisted. The booklet gives the birth date as Sept. 18 and the homestead year as 1898; the paper says Sept. 13 and 1899.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Then on to Edmonton and to Camp Shilo, Brandon in May 1940.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: In Aug. they headed for Halifax. There were 5 troopships in the harbour . and they had to wait for them all to load. He sailed on the Duchess of York, the rolling Duchess.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: “The Hood” was an escort vessel which was later sank by the Bismark. They had few tense moments when a merchant vessel past through the convoy and the Hood had its guns trained on it.( No radar in those days). They landed at Greenock and proudly wore their bright blue shoulder flashes. Their uniform consisted of khaki trousers and tunic, a greatcoat to mid calf all made of itchy wool cloth. They had a khaki rain cape that also served as a ground sheet. They were issued a gas mask in a case with a steel helmet attached that went with them everywhere even on a date. They also had a small pack for personal effects and a large pack for sleeping blanket, socks etc. and a set of mess tins.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: They went to Farnborough where Clayton could see the glass house {Army Prison} from his window. They rioted there , their strips covered with rain capes because the Colonel was shitty, and the officers were selling the rations on the black-market making the food inadequate. This remedied the situation.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text:
On to Bognor Regis in the vital year of 1941 where they were billeted on the seafront in the commandeered guest houses. They had 6 lbs guns with 1914 ammunition in the pill boxes along the coast which they manned. For 160 men they had 60 rifles and 50 rounds of ammunition per rifle and 2 Lewis machine guns {1st, war} with 500 rounds per gun. They had 5-2lb guns , 3 with barrels and 2 without and no ammunition for either. The other 100 men were to stand in the slit trench and clap their hands. That was how they were to stop the Germans if they invaded Briton!!

Gradually things got better and training was the order of every day.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On to Steyning in 1942 a beautiful market town in Sussex. He went to a gas course on Salisbury Plains with the British Army , and a man-handling course at Lyde. Here 20 men had to man handle a gun weighing 3 ton. through a pit 25ft,deep and run 3 miles to town and back still towing the gun. After 5 days of this they were in shape and would throw a rope over the white cliffs of Dover and go for a swim in the Channel after.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text: “They didn’t plan on taking the anti-tank divisions across for the raid until later,” remembered Brown. “We lost so many soldiers... it’s hard to comprehend.”

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On Sept 17th. 1943 he got married[ a woman handing course]. Thousand bombers were a sight over head daily as Briton got on the offensive.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: From there they went to a holding area by Dover, no leaves, no writing or phoning. Clayton went on the Advance party to London to load equipment on the freighter. When the troops came they slept on board too in hammocks. The buzz-bombs were active one hit a tank landing craft nearby.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: He went to France when they had enough room to land about July 1st, The battery had waterproofed their 8x6lb and 4x17lb guns pulled by 4x4 quads which held the 7 man crew and ammunition . It was lifted by cranes on to rafts as big as our garden with 4 outboard motors on. They went to a holding unit where the vehicles were un-waterproofed, Clayton being the last one off the boat, got there when everyone had left.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Catching up to the battery who were in the 2nd, line of defense, the heavy artillery were firing over them, a spectacular sight. This was at Carpiquet airport outside Caen. To give the impression of strength a field was filled with inflated rubber tanks. They had to watch for french women snipers, one hiding behind a chimney was brought down by machine gun fire.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: They then moved through Caen to Ifs. They followed the S.Sask regiment infantry into battle there, the target was 1 500yds over open country, the Essex-Scottish made about 1000yds and the FMR's [Fusiliers of Montreal] on the left were fired on by a German tiger tank and they broke rank and fled. Their officer running behind them saying in french “Stop or I'll shoot” and he should have. Clayton never had any use for the french after that. This left the flank open for the Germans to shoot them from behind. They were wiped out .They lost 4 guns, 4 trucks and 23 men killed or wounded out of 39 of the K troop. Clayton was lucky and went to J troop and any men that were left. They were in action every day .Once they fixed bayonets because the Germans were over the hill ahead of them. Tha Germans were stopped by the Typhoon planes with rockets. They found out later there were 4 Panther divisions in front of them, the cream of the German army which they were to draw off the Americans so they could make their big push.

quotes.source: From John S. Edmondson and R.D. Edmondson, “The Pawns of War: A Personal Account of the Attack on Verrières Ridge by The South Saskatchewan Regiment, 20 July 1944,” Canadian Military History 14, no. 4 (2005). John Edmondson commanded a South Saskatchewan company that day.
quotes.text:
Our own Battalion supporting arms were the Battalion Mortar Platoon, Captain W.G.A. Lane OC, and the six 6-pounder anti-tank guns, Captain G.E. Colgate, OC. To this were added 17-pounder anti-tank guns from the “K” Troop, 23rd Battery, 2nd Anti Tank Regiment.

As I passed over the crest south of the St. Martin-de-Fontenay crossroad, I saw 17-pounder anti-tank guns being knocked out. As the first was being towed into position, it was hit by enemy fire and was aflame before it even stopped. On stopping, the crew bailed out and they were all on fire.

The attached “K” Troop, 23rd Battery 2nd Anti-Tank Regiment reported their four 17-pounder guns lost, and 7 personnel killed and some missing. The “some missing” as it turned out were 7 personnel who were found to be in hospital on 31 July.

This is an eyewitness account of Clayton's own troop being destroyed, by an officer of the battalion it was supporting. The guns were on call to come forward once the infantry reached their objectives; they were hit as they arrived. The article also says the Sherbrooke Fusiliers tanks, part of Gordon's 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade, supported the attack, with their headquarters tanks in the orchard on the west side of Ifs.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, 20th Battery, 2 Antitank (A/T), 2nd Canadian Infantry Division 1939-1945: A Personal View (2025), p. 68, on July 21
quotes.text:
In the downward slope leaving St André sur Orne and leading into St Martin de Fontenay seven Panther tanks came in out of the mist accompanied by infantry. Major AC Lennon and the Camerons were in a small orchard in St. André and felt the 6 pounders of the 23rd Bty Troop they had with them could not reach the tanks. He called for a 17 pounder.

At this point a 6 pounder crew of the 23rd Bty in the orchard, having had their gun destroyed, made towards the 17 pdr. One of its crew, Bdr Grassick, under fire all the way, made it to the hit 17 pounder only to find it not working. He managing to get its firing mechanism working by freeing it with an axe and he destroyed another Panther before withdrawing.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, p. 70, on July 22 and 23
quotes.text:
On the 22nd of July the 2nd Division was hunkered down on the edge of Verriéres Ridge. The 2 A/T was with the 5 CIB and the Camerons in St. André and east. All units reported counter attacks from the enemy.

That morning it was raining and the day saw a lot of mortar fire and sniping. Reports were that between the rain and the smoke nothing could be seen until the enemy was right on top of them.

23rd Bty lost Capt HFW Smith (died the next day from stomach wounds) and Gnr Chillwell were wounded from mortar fire and evacuated.

Operation Atlantic was over. As of July 23rd, 5 days after activation in Normandy, the 2 A/T had 25 killed, 46 wounded, 13 missing and 17 evacuated for medical reasons.

quotes.source: Award recommendation for M1026 Bdr George Albert Grassick, 2 Cdn A.Tk Regt RCA (LAC, reproduced in Young, Figure 55)
quotes.text:
On 21 Jul 44, Bdr Grassick was the NCO i/c a 6 pr A.Tk gun sited in the Camerons of Canada area at ST ANDRE SUR ORNE. His gun had been knocked out. A nearby 17 pr gun which had been brought forward to snipe at harrassing Panther Tanks had received a direct hit which jammed the breech, and the crew had withdrawn under orders. Bdr Grassick, without regard to his personal safety and while under heavy fire, crawled to the 17 pr and by breaking the semi-automatic gear was able to fire the gun, which he did single-handed until he ran out of ammunition, destroying one tank and obtaining hits on others. By his individula courage, Bdr Grassick was an example to all troops at hand and his single-handed fighting of the damaged 17 pr was a contribution to the success of the previous action.

In plain English: Grassick was in charge of one of the 23rd Battery's 6-pounders in the Camerons' orchard. When it was knocked out, he crawled under fire to a damaged 17-pounder whose crew had been ordered out. The gun normally opened its own breech after each shot; he broke that mechanism so he could work it by hand, and fired it alone until the ammunition ran out. One Panther destroyed, others hit. The margin names Lt. Col. H.E. Murray, the regiment's CO, as the officer recommending it, and appears to read "Mention in Despatches".

"M1026" is his service number. The M prefix was given to men enlisting in Alberta, so Grassick was very likely an Alberta man in Clayton's battery.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On to capture Falaise the Canadians from one side the Yanks from the other and the Germans in the middle. They slowly closed the gap, and 100,000 or more Germans were killed and 195,000 captured of S.S. troops ,Hitlers prime. Here they were strafed by the Americans Lightings because they did not think they could advance that fast. The Canadians got there first.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, pp. 82 and 84, on Operation Totalize, August 7 and 8, 1944
quotes.text:
The 23rd Bty reported being within 200yds of the impact zone during the bombing. There were reports of bombs falling short and onto Canadian and British positions.

23rd Bty J Troop was at Fontenay le Marmion and came under 88 fire and lost 1 gun and 2 vehicles. Combat was very close as 1 quad was put out of action by a hand grenade and 6 prisoners were taken.

The bombing was the night of Aug. 7, when over a thousand RAF bombers hit both sides of the Caen–Falaise road ahead of the Canadian advance. J troop is the troop the booklet says Clayton joined after Ifs, so this is likely his own troop, a little over two weeks later. A "quad" was the gun tractor that towed the gun and carried its crew.

brown.headline: Holding the pocket with Maj. Currie

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: In Oct the Americans on the right, Canadians on the left and a pocket of 20,000 Germans between them. He was attached to an attack group. consisting of a squadron of tanks, 170 infantry, R.E.C.E. Group & K troop anti/tank which had 4 guns 38 men their job was to cut across the top of the pocket to the American lines. They got half way across and the Germans held them up. They owned 2 streets and the Germans had the rest . The Germans shot up a tank at the front door of the house they were in .Sniping was bad ,the civilians were still in there. So 24 hr truce was called so the civilians could get out baby buggies and all. Maybe some snipers too. The Germans put in a night attack and the tank corp called for field artillery and they laid a circular barrage around the 2 block area they were in. Very exciting and scary. It took a week, they lost a gun crew to enemy fire. The 3rd, day C.T. took the Jeep with the batman to the edge of their lines. Crossing open territory the enemy held they saw an armored half-track upside down in the ditch and they made a run for it, On arrival they were asked how we got there and they said speed and guts and no sense. The tank corps commander was Maj. Currie who had won the V.C. earlier and was fearless.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text:
Under the command of Major David Currie, Brown and the rest of the army began the hard fight to take Falais.

“The Germans cut us off halfway. We had to stay put for 10 days,” recalled Brown. “We had two streets of Falais and the Germans had the rest.”

“So he walked in front of one of the tanks and said ‘knock that building down, knock that one down.’ That’s the way he walked down the street.

“Why he never got shot by a sniper, I don’t know. I’m sure the tank scared them. He deserved the Victoria Cross.”

Currie and his small force of 175 men, of which Brown was a part, destroyed seven German tanks, killed or wounded 800 Germans, and took more than 1,000 prisoners.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Then to the Seine and Rouen, heavy fighting and he lost his officer and signaler. The Americans had captured a bridge at Elbeuf which would hold the guns where they crossed. On arrival at Rouen he learned his major had died, pushed out of a upstairs window and fell in a rain barrel (Killed in action) !! They were party to the shelling and capture of a giant pill-box with only a slit above ground. From this they took 129 prisoners and 2 women and there were 6 floors underground- such were their fortifications.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Then they were given the job of recapturing Dieppe, going in from the backside. To celebrate a march past was held 6 abreast and they could have all been wiped out by one lone plane.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: After a long move heading for Dunkirk, shooting up the Jerries who were holed out there. they moved up toward Antwerp where the 1000 bombers pulling gliders on there way to Arnhem were overhead.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: The battle of the Schelt and a bitter battle all the way to the Walcheren Islands to make a passage way for the ships and the supplies to get to Antwerp. One night a plane shot them up because a gun had opened fire on it. From Beveland to the causeway and the English commandoes took over there.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, p. 104, on October 12, 1944
quotes.text:
October 12 a quiet day. Many of the Troops without #22 wireless set. Shelling and mortaring on all Btys throughout the day. 20th Bty back under 5CIB. 23rd Bty K Troop M/1003 Sgt Robert Earl Austin and Gnr Halliday wounded by a sniper. Sgt Austin died the next day in hospital, leaving his parents in Calgary and his wife Dorothy in Red Deer.

Austin's M prefix means he enlisted in Alberta, and his number sits close to Grassick's (M1026), which points to an early 1939 enlistment like Clayton's. A K troop sergeant with a wife in Red Deer is very likely someone Clayton knew.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, p. 108, on October 23 and 24, 1944
quotes.text:
The 23rd also commanding the 18th Bty in support of the SSR (J Troop), FMR (K Troop) and Camerons as they advance.

23rd Bty with 5CIB, a number of buildings and chimney OP destroyed.

So on Oct. 23 J troop was with the South Saskatchewan Regiment and K troop with the Fusiliers Mont-Royal. The "chimney OP" is the brick-works chimney K troop knocked down on Oct. 24 (see the war diary below). OP means observation post: the Germans were using it as a lookout.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Through Bergen Op Zoom east to Nijmegen but it had been taken by the paratroopers and gliders so they moved on to Groesbeek for most of the winter.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text:
Housed in an old store where they found a ham in the chimney and 100lbs. Of sugar. With the batman they blew off the lock of the safe, and found new dutch gilders printed in England for the paratroopers. They were able to use real dishes and it snowed!!

Then the battle of the Bulge took place, the Germans threatened they would break threw the Canadian lines but they broke threw the American lines and German planes flew 100ft overhead. Just before Xmas. Christmas 1944 they had all the trimmings in Nyjmegen.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On Feb.7th. they started into Germany. 1000 bomber raids had gone on ahead into Cleeve and Goch. which were completely destroyed by bomber command. They had now been equipped with new self-propelled 17lb guns which used a crew of 5. They had 2 sorts of shells, one was armour-piercing which could pierce 10inches of armour plating and traveled at 3200ft. (2/3 mile) per second and the other was high explosive and they could fire about 5 rounds a minute. The Germans broke the dams north of Cleeve and caused a big flood to roads etc. and there were 1000 guns behind firing , a big noise .It started a 12.PM. till the attach went in at 8.am. Some drunken anti-tank gunners fired too. There shells were landing about 22 miles back of the German lines. They strung grenades across the road to keep the enemy tanks from crossing at night. The infantry piled them next day behind a tree and the colonel of the infantry went behind the tree in his jeep and was blown sky-high.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text:
Their weapons to fight the Nazi forces were self-propelled guns. They were similar to tanks, but they had an open turret and could rotate only slightly.

“The driver had to move the entire gun when the target moved,” said Brown.

“We rarely saw the other SPs (self-propelled guns) in our battery because each SP had to stick with a platoon assigned,” said Brown. “We didn’t function as a combined unit.”

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, p. 115, on February 1945
quotes.text: The 18th and 23rd Btys had been brought up to Groesbeek with the 153rd Scottish (30 Corps) passing through. Kleve was taken the 10th of February. On the 18th February the Regiment was concentrated at Materborn on the south east edge of Kleve.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On to the Hochwald forest where he saw them getting water from a slough with a dead horse in it . They just threw in a couple of tablets and it was drinkable. Once his officer went to a meeting and they waited under tree. When they left a carrier took their place and was blown to bits, they had been sitting on a landmine.. He also tells of sleeping in a chicken house ,dead tired ,he woke up with something on his chest, and there was a rat sitting upright. He swatted at it and the whole place was alive.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: On to Zanten where he got the bayonet we have from a house. They had sent in a company of infantry because it was reported to be clear and when they had got through a narrow opening into the town, the German paratroopers opened up and killed them all. Then the British Wessex and Canadians had to launch a full scale attach to take the town

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text:
He holds up a picture of a dashing young soldier standing confidently in front of a self-propelled artillery gun.

“That’s me,” he said, smiling slightly. “It was taken in Germany towards the close of the war.”

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: They crossed the Rhine at Rees, the Americans below them. The landing craft from the coast were brought to get across the river.

quotes.source: From Bruce W. Young, p. 120, on March 28 to 30, 1945
quotes.text:
On March 28 the Regiment began crossing the Rhine. Initially the 23rd Bty with the 6th Brigade at 2300 and the next morning the 20th Bty with the 5th Brigade.

On March 30th the 23rd Bty I troop lost a quad. Both I troop and K troop returned fire on churches being used as observation posts. They were in constant contact with the enemy past Ulft and Veldhunter.

Clayton's battery was the first of the regiment across, at 11 p.m. on March 28. The churches were being used as German lookouts, which made their steeples targets.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: They made a push straight to Groningen in Holland. This is where a trooper, drunk, came on parade with a Dutch girl on his arm and guilders flying. Someone had blown up the bank. Then the 1st and 5th Canadians from Italy joined them. They met slight resistance north to the coast of Holland.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Then on to Oldenburg. in heavy fighting they were taking the area cross road to cross road. An error by the medium artillery caused them to be shelled and they hid under the democrats and the batman had a helmet full of eggs which he kept safe. This is where the war ended. May 1945. His troop had 47 men wounded or killed. Clayton and batman were unscathed, He started with 38 men others were replacements and were known as the jinxed K troop. There had been 170,000 Canadian troops in the field and 67,000 supply troops.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: They moved to the FreisenIslands and stood guard on German prisoners for about a week and then moved back to a holding unit in Holland and started rotation leaves.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text:
He went to Eccleshall and visited brother Tom at an air force base in Yorkshire. He had not seen him since 1940 and Lynda had already left for Canada. Clayton slept in sheets for the first time in 6 years.

He was not informed of his repatriation to Canada so he had to return to Germany. He waited a month for the next rotation to come up then on to Aldershot and waited.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: Back to Grennock and home on the Ile de France in 5 days in Aug. There were about 3000 on board and General Crerar. He landed at Halifax and 5 days later in Calgary by troop train.

quotes.source: From the Red Deer Advocate, Aug. 15, 1945, “Local boys on their way home” (photo caption)
quotes.text: These three Alberta veterans were photographed on Board the “Ile de France,” which docked at Halifax on August 5. They have all been welcomed home since. From left to right they are: Tpr. Clifford Hooey, Condor, who was a prisoner of war for nearly three years, having been taken prisoner at Dieppe; Sgt. Alton Morris, Grande Prairie, and Sgt. Clayton Brown, son of Mrs. L. E. Brown, Red Deer.

quotes.source: From the Red Deer Advocate, June 13, 1945, “Local Happenings”
quotes.text:
Mrs. Clayton T. Brown arrived Tuesday from Wincote Lodge, Staffordshire, England, and will make her home with Mrs. L. E. Brown, Michener Hill.

So Lynda reached Red Deer first, on June 12, nearly two months before Clayton landed at Halifax. She was waiting for him at his mother's house on Michener Hill.

quotes.source: From Lynda's booklet
quotes.text: He was demobbed on Sept 12th. 1945. He had weighed in at 132 lbs. And weighed out at 132 ½ lbs. He then stayed on in the reserve force till moving to Lacombe.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “The tank killers”
quotes.text:
To this day, Brown can’t understand how he made it through alive when so many of his friends didn’t.

“We were more a family than a unit,” he recalls. “There was a real sense of camaraderie and friendship.”

“We all looked out for each other.”

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, “Lacombe remembers its veterans” (photo caption)
quotes.text: Sgt. of Arms Clayton Brown listens during the Rememberance Day ceremonies that hundreds attended at the Lacombe Memorial Centre on Nov.11.

brown.headline: Meanwhile: Gordon leaves the army in Calgary

quotes.source: From The Quiet Service of Captain Gordon Carlyle Sweet, M.B.E., the family history drawn from his service file
quotes.text: Gordon Carlyle Sweet was born on February 23, 1914, in Yellow Grass, Saskatchewan—a small prairie town southeast of Regina, named for the wild grass that covered the plains before the plows came.

quotes.source: From The Quiet Service of Captain Gordon Carlyle Sweet, M.B.E., the family history drawn from his service file
quotes.text: He participated in C.O.T.C. (Canadian Officers’ Training Corps) parades and completed annual training in 1938–39. This militia service would prove decisive when he enlisted for the war.

quotes.source: From the Edmonton Bulletin, May 4, 1940, p. 24
quotes.text: Sweet, Gordon Carlyle, Lacombe

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, Sept. 12, 1940, p. 1
quotes.text: Under the command of Major G. G. Wannop of Wetaskiwin and Captain W. A. Henry of Bentley, members from Lacombe are: Staff Sergeant G. M. Ramsay, Sergeant Gordon Sweet, ...

sweet.headline: Running the dispensary at Sarcee Camp

quotes.source: From the Edmonton Bulletin, Aug. 11, 1941, p. 8
quotes.text: A large dispensary, in charge of Sgt. G. Sweet, Lacombe, is filled with medicine of every description and is entirely up-to-date.

quotes.source: From The Quiet Service of Captain Gordon Carlyle Sweet, M.B.E., the family history drawn from his service file
quotes.text: He listed his trade as “Pharmaceutical Chemist,” his next of kin as his mother Mae, and his address as Lacombe, Alberta.

sweet.headline: Six weeks from private to officer

quotes.source: From the order that made him an officer, quoted in The Quiet Service
quotes.text: To be 2/Lt (Qr Mr) 14 Nov 41 — M 29601 A/WO ll SWEET G.C. (RCAMC) (17th Field Ambulance RCAMC).

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, June 30, 1943, p. 6
quotes.text: In a cable received this (Wednesday) morning by his parents, Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Sweet, their son, Capt. Gordon Sweet, sent word that he has arrived safely overseas. Capt. Sweet is attached to the Canadian Army Medical Corps.

quotes.source: From The Quiet Service of Captain Gordon Carlyle Sweet, M.B.E., the family history drawn from his service file, on Mel Barr's account
quotes.text: Their first night in France, they were attacked by the Luftwaffe. Without time to dig slit trenches, they spent the night under their RCAMC truck.

quotes.source: From the Lacombe Globe, Nov. 30, 1944, p. 3
quotes.text: CAPTAIN GORDON SWEET of the Canadian Army Medical Corps, son of Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Sweet, Lacombe, who is seeing a lot of action just now in the big advance of the Canadian Forces in Belgium and Holland.

sweet.headline: Member of the Order of the British Empire

quotes.source: From the Edmonton Bulletin, Dec. 14, 1945, pp. 1 and 3
quotes.text: Capt. G. C. / Sweet, Lacombe

quotes.source: Gordon's own words, Department of Veterans Affairs interview, Calgary, April 9, 1946 (from The Quiet Service)
quotes.text:
I am taking over father’s drug store as my father is retiring.

The purpose of this counselling interview has been explained to me and I consider it unnecessary as I am taking over my father’s drug store.

quotes.source: From the Edmonton Bulletin, Apr. 10, 1946, p. 9
quotes.text: Capt. G. C. Sweet, RCAMC, Lacombe.

quotes.source: His statutory declaration, as quoted in The Quiet Service

sweet.headline: Hospital Auxiliary, I.O.D.E. and the skating club

close_by.title: about 23 km apart
close_by.text: They grew up in neighbouring towns in central Alberta, Clayton in Red Deer and Gordon in Lacombe, on the same rail line and less than half an hour apart. Gordon was six years older. No record shows whether they knew each other then.

close_by.title: about 5 km apart
close_by.text: The closest they came in the war. On July 20, 1944, Clayton's K troop was destroyed at Ifs, at the foot of Verrières Ridge. The attack Clayton's troop was supporting had tanks of the Sherbrooke Fusiliers, one of the three regiments of Gordon's 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade, and their headquarters tanks sat in the orchard on the west side of Ifs. Gordon's field ambulance was the brigade's medical unit, set up behind them taking in the wounded. Whether any of Clayton's troop passed through Gordon's unit isn't recorded.

b: Holding the pocket with Maj. Currie
close_by.title: the same battle
close_by.text: In Operation Totalize, the night attack south from Caen on Aug. 7 and 8, 1944, the tanks of Gordon's brigade went in with Clayton's 2nd Division. Clayton's J troop was in close fighting at Fontenay-le-Marmion on Aug. 8. Both units then pushed on toward Falaise.

close_by.title: about 18 km apart
close_by.text: Late August 1944: Clayton's division fought through the forest south of Rouen and crossed at Elbeuf, while Gordon's brigade crossed the Seine nearby on Aug. 28.

close_by.title: within about 25 km
close_by.text: February and March 1945: both were in First Canadian Army's push through the Reichswald and Hochwald into Germany, around Cleve.

close_by.title: the same crossing, a day apart
close_by.text: Clayton's 23rd Battery crossed the Rhine at Rees at 11 p.m. on March 28, 1945, the first of his regiment across. Gordon's brigade crossed at Rees on March 29.

close_by.title: the same town
close_by.text: After the war both made their lives in Lacombe, Gordon running Sweet's Pharmacy and Clayton raising his family a few streets away. Their children later married.
